articles.title: Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin , two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri , a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.
Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.
Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.
It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.
The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016 . He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.
Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

articles.title: Study: 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers rival Denmark’s emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website , comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.
Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group .

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.
“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July .
Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September , “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times .

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

articles.title: Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media , “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times . Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.
Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement . Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post , writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.
I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.
“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

articles.title: What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage , rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.
Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.
Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.
When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.
Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.
The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.
The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.
The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold . Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

articles.title: Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’
articles.author: Mary Jo Foley
paras: It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS .”
Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.
The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders , published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.
The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race : In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.
Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

articles.title: Lawmakers Turn to a 'Highway Use Fee' to Bolster Sagging Transportation Budget
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: State legislators who have been trying in vain for years to find a more sustainable funding source to replace Washington's waning gas tax are set to try a new tactic in 2027. House Transportation committee chair Jake Fey (D-27th, Tacoma) is gearing up to introduce a new "highway use fee" to help salvage a state transportation budget that continues to invest more in the expansion of the highway network than in the preservation and and maintenance of existing infrastructure.

Thanks to increased fuel efficiency and some degree of compact urban planning, gasoline usage in Washington is never expected to return to a 2018 highwater mark again, with projections instead predicting a steady decline. Revenue from the state gas tax – currently set at 56.5 cents per gallon – is expected to decline in future years as well, even after a six-cent gas tax increase in 2025 that was paired with a future 2% annual inflation adjustment.

This fall, Rep. Fey has been holding a series of "listening sessions" with different groups around the state involved in transportation planning about the highway use fee, though the proposal has been floating around for some time. Lawmakers are expecting a bill to be filed in the lead up to the 2027 session, which begins January 11.

While some details are still being ironed out – hence the listening sessions – the broad contours of a highway use fee are clear. Drivers renewing their car tabs would be charged an additional fee if the published fuel economy standard of their vehicle falls above a certain level. The more fuel-efficient that vehicle is, the higher the fee. In Virginia, where the existing highway use fee is seen as the model for Washington State, that level is 25 miles per gallon. Only vehicles weighing 10,000 pounds or less are set to be covered, taking freight vehicles out of the equation.

Virginia's fees currently range from around $7 for a 25-mpg vehicle to approximately $75 for some of the most fuel-efficient hybrids. Right now, it's not clear whether or how Washington would adjust existing hybrid and electric vehicle fees, which are currently $225 for all vehicles with an electric range of at least 30 miles.

"I would call a bit of a modernization of our transportation system revenues," Fey said last week in a presentation at the Puget Sound Regional Council, speaking to local elected officials. "We are bound and have been utilizing user fees, whether it's tax on fuel or whether it's fees on vehicles, as our primary revenue source. We do have what one could call a highway use fee in terms of existing electric and hybrid [vehicle] fees, but we do still have a fuel tax revenue gap."

Fey noted he is planning to advance the highway use fee with the support of several other legislators including Rep. Julia Reed (D-36th, Queen Anne), vice chair of the House's transportation committee, and Senator Javier Valdez (D-46th, Northeast Seattle).

Though legislators turned to debt this year to balance the transportation budget, issuing $500 million in bonds to keep the 520 bridge replacement project on track in addition to $800 million for overdue bridge and highway upkeep, the work of transportation budget writers is expected to remain challenging. According to the state's Office of Financial Management, transportation revenues are currently expected to be $599 million lower through 2031 compared to the budget that was approved this past March.

In designing a program that charges drivers more for having fuel-efficient vehicles, Fey's proposal will likely not earn him much acclaim among environmental advocates looking to encourage electric vehicle adoption. But he framed his proposal as helping to make the question of who contributes to maintaining transportation infrastructure more fair.

"We've got people who are generally at the lower economic part of our economy that can't afford a new car, a fuel-efficient car for the most part, they're paying more in gas taxes than someone that can afford to buy a very highly efficient vehicle that would be unaffordable for many people," Fey said. "So this is trying to create a little bit more balance and fairness in terms of who pays into the system."

While likely still a heavy lift during a time of heavy scrutiny on additional taxes, the push for a highway use fee will represent a pivot away from a per-mile user fee that looked to be the primary path toward a long-term gas tax replacement. Concerns had been raised with the privacy impacts of creating a road usage charge on top of cost impacts, but it would have also been a significantly heavier lift for the state to stand up.
Fey said that unlike a per-mile road usage charge, a highway use fee could be in place by late 2028 if it were approved next year.

While more difficult to implement, a road usage charge would be fairer from the perspective of scaling fees to mileage, so drivers who rack up tons of miles on state roads pay their fair share, while people who drive sparingly get rewarded relative to their peers. In comparison, an annual highway use fee is a blunt instrument that does not create an incentive to drive less.

One major element of the behind-the-scenes wrangling to come will be how exactly revenues from a highway use fee get distributed. While the majority of gas tax revenue currently goes to the state transportation budget, slices of those dollars do get handed out to cities and counties dealing with transportation funding struggles of their own. Whether there should be some degree of local pass-through – a familiar discussion to anyone following the transportation funding debate at the King County Council earlier this year – will be hotly debated.

Ultimately, a highway use fee is not likely to generate revenue on par with the gas tax. Virginia's current system generates around $100 million per year, compared to the $1.5 billion per year that is generated by Washington's motor vehicle fuel tax.

But it could act as a stopgap, giving lawmakers another tool as some major highway projects look to be coming down the pike, including the replacement of the westbound US 2 trestle in Everett and I-5 through the Nisqually Delta near Olympia. Of course, if state transportation revenue does continue to largely help to fund big-ticket highway projects at the expense of maintaining state and local transportation infrastructure, the legislature might end up in the exact same spot in just a few years, searching for new revenue tools that will enable them to keep pace.

articles.title: As Annapurna Cafe prepares for a big 2027 — and bigger 2028 — it is saying goodbye to Yeti Bar
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: It’s your final week to enjoy the Yeti Bar .
Annapurna Cafe’s Broadway-level hangout next to the west Capitol Hill Station entrance is shutting down after a short, unsuccessful search for a buyer.

Annapurna’s Roshita Shrestha says the decision came down to costs. The closure of the bar comes as Annapurna continues serving below with a big year ahead preparing for a move to a new Broadway space.

CHS reported here on Shrestha and Sujan Sharma’s preparations for the move into a commercial condominium space they purchased on the north end of Broadway years ago to be ready for the 23-year-old restaurant’s eventual relocation.

Annapurna’s current home has long been lined up for redevelopment as a six-story, 50-unit mixed-use building under plans first approved a decade ago . That project was put on ice due to landmarks protections . Any new development plan will need to incorporate preservation of the building’s historic proportions, look, and feel.
The extra time has allowed Annapurna to stay put at 1833 Broadway and will give the Himalayan joint even more time to manage its move to the bigger, better North Broadway space.

Shrestha said that they are starting the paperwork for the overhaul of the new location this fall but the plan is for Annapurna to make the move north in the spring of 2028, leaving 2027 as a year of preparation and construction. In the meantime, Annapurna will continue serving at 1833 Broadway and might continue operating a lunch and takeout business in the space even after the move depending on how long the old building will remain standing.
Star Sushi can continue its run in the space lined up for Annapurna until the buildout and upgrade work takes place in the coming year.

Yeti Bar is less fortunate. Annapurna first opened the street-level sibling bar in 2015 with hopes of launching a higher margin approach to its flavors of Nepal with cocktails and happy hour bites. It was also a celebration of survival as Annapurna shook off the dust from years of light rail construction on the block.

Like many old Capitol Hill favorites experimenting with new Capitol Hill formats, Yeti Bar provided new energy but didn’t hugely change Annapurna’s business prospects. Still, Shrestha says, after 11 years, the bar has had its regulars who will be sad to see it go. She is planning to preserve some of the art from the space to take along through Annapurna’s changes. The final night at Yeti Bar is slated for Saturday.
After that, the Annapurna family will be looking at the year ahead and counting down the days until the spring of 2028.
Annapurna remains open at 1833 Broadway. Follow @annapurnacafeseattle for updates.

articles.title: Suspicious item locks down East Precinct — UPDATE: Reopened
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A suspicious item had the area around the East Precinct locked down Monday.
Seattle Police has not released information on the shutdown but officers at the scene said it involved a suspicious item.
12th Ave between Pine and Pike was closed to traffic and pedestrians during the closure that remained in place as of just before 12:30 PM.
UPDATE : SPD confirmed the closure is related to a suspicious item — “a package left near the precinct.”
UPDATE 1:10 PM : SPD reports the area has reopened and that “there is no threat the public.”
We’ll follow up to learn more about the incident.

articles.title: Flash Gordon, half the minimum wage, and lightbulbs — How WFLM plans to make the Egyptian Theatre revival last
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: How does a gang of four movie lovers plan to keep a revived Egyptian Theatre thriving on Capitol Hill? Ben Redde r tells CHS it is about accessibility and affordability.

“It’s still kind of repulsive to see how expensive it is to enjoy living in this place,” Redder says about the city of Seattle circa 2026. “Our idea is ‘half of minimum wage’ — a half hour of your time is worth two hours of our time.”

Redder and the folks that formed WFLM to organize the reopening of the classic Capitol Hill movie theater aren’t running a charity. We Friggin’ Love Movies is not a flipping charity. It’s a business but one that film lovers Redder, Elias Savage, Scotty Wright, and Lanna Hed believe should be shaped by accessibility for as many people as possible with affordable tickets and a slate of flicks to appeal to brows high and low.
“You bet your ass that Flash Gordon (1980) is going to be on that screen,” Redder promises.

The schedule will be eclectic, mixing cult classics, film nut favorites, Joe Bob Briggs -approved schlock, and, importantly, screenings and events that mix the silver screen with live conversations and interactions with filmmakers and more in the Egyptian’s auditorium.
First run screenings will be a rarity but Redder said the Egyptian will be ready if special event opportunities come up to debut the right films.
The new era at the Egyptian will begin as mostly a weekends-only schedule with a few Tuesday night appearances of WFLM’s Classified Cinema series.
“There’s only four of us and we all have other gigs,” Redder said.

Opening night for the WFLM Egyptian revival will give you an idea of what is coming with a planned twin bill pairing 1940s dance drama The Red Shoes and 1980s b-boying and b-girling classic Breakin’ 2: Electric Boogaloo .

The curtain officially rises on the new era the night of Friday, December 4th. Tickets for the special event will be $20. A DVD swap for lovers of physical media will kick off the fun starting at 6 PM.
The following weeks will bring Midnight Movies and more including holiday events that mix “traditional and non-traditional” movie going experiences — and maybe Santa.
CHS reported here on the “soft opening” schedule of Midnight Movies already lined up as WFLM takes over operating the historic theater.

WFLM and the E Pine theater building’s owner Seattle Central have been working out details of a long-term lease for the venue that has been available for events but hasn’t been serving the public regularly since a major water pipe break damaged the landmark former Masonic Temple in November 2024.

WFLM has been part of this year’s pop-ups in the Egyptian as Seattle Central opened a schedule of one-time showings and special screenings to light the theater back up after a long closure following the water pipe break and the exit of SIFF .
The school has been looking for a new long-term tenant for the theater that has been showcasing arthouse, classic, and international cinema since 1980.

The group says it plans to operate the Egyptian similarly to Santa Ana’s Frida Cinema with programming centering on repertory cinema, crowd favorites, forgotten titles, and the return of late-night midnight movie screenings.
Seattle Central says the agreement runs through June and can be renewed annually.
The immediate future of the theater will remain focused on film — but the school says the space could serve wider arts and culture needs.

“Our goal is to support and showcase local arts through the use of the Egyptian,” a spokesperson tells CHS. “While a cinema is one potential use, Seattle Central was open to a range of opportunities that would contribute to the city’s arts and cultural community.”
Redder said the lease is significant and the team will be working hard to make the revival last.
“We didn’t get a sweetheart deal,” he says.

The WFLM gang knows movies and are core to the Seattle film scene. Redder brings operations experience having managed Cinerama and The Egyptian in the past. He describes the awe he still feels inside the space. “The auditorium is stunning. It is gorgeous,” he says.
The team has been making small improvements for the re-opening. Simple things like changing out lightbulbs for the same color temperature throughout the space.
Other projects including paperwork to secure a new liquor license for the theater.

There is other work that needs to be done and lots of talk about “the previous tenant” and how it treated the building. Lots of cool old features from the theater’s past were simply pulled from the walls over the past decade.

One project being sorted out is how best to revive the poster wells on the outside of the building to showcase current and upcoming showings. They’re trying to figure out some DIY solutions to using the spaces before long-term electrical work would happen to light the posters and flyers up.
The marquee and awning have also seen better days. For now, WFLM is taking a “lo-fi” approach.
“We taped over the previous tenant’s name,” Redder said.

WFLM currently isn’t planning any “crowdfunding” campaigns or donation drives to fund more significant upgrades. Redder says to expect an opportunity to get involved opening night and during the theater’s screenings. Some film lovers have already pitched in.
“Let’s just say some people will get ‘popcorn for life,'” Redder said.

The first goal was achieved this summer getting WFLM programming on the Egyptian’s big screen. A second will come with December 4th’s grand opening. The most important goal will be to last the first year. Redder and the WFLM team are hoping their focus on making the theater a space for everybody can be the start.
“We’re just a bunch of nerds that love going to the movies,” Redder said. “We relish when going to the movies was an experience in and of itself.”
WFLM Egyptian is screening midnight movies and more at 805 E Pine. Learn more at wflmseattle.com .

articles.title: Marathon Monday for Seattle Council budget session after Friday’s slow start and key pullbacks including debate over Fire Pension Fund and raiding JumpStart
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Seattle City Council members are bracing for a potential all-night session Monday after falling roughly three hours behind schedule during an eight-hour Select Budget Committee marathon on Friday.

While the council led by budget chair Dan Strauss unanimously adopted a 126-item consent package of budget amendments on Friday afternoon, council members were forced to pull 16 proposals for separate debate leaving dozens of individual votes and standalone budget bills unresolved heading into Monday’s continuation meeting.

Friday’s slowdown stemmed from procedural pauses to resolve agenda conflicts, nearly two hours of spoken public testimony from more than 100 speakers on cooperative preschools, surveillance, and housing, and a line-by-line review of 142 items in Strauss’s unprecedentedly stuffed-full consent package.

It also is representative of the council’s push to tap extra funding as members try to restore funding for programs they champion and their district priorities amid Mayor Katie Wilson’s budget proposal designed to wipe away a $175 million deficit by slowing expensive undertakings like police hiring.

Under Council budget rules, any member can pull an item from the consent package which passes with one combined vote, forcing the item onto the individual-vote docket. Pulling an item does not kill it but it strips away automatic consensus, forcing sponsors to defend the spending on the record, opening the door to competing amendments or technical rewrites, and requiring a standalone roll-call vote where a simple majority is needed to survive. Among the 16 proposals pulled for Monday’s individual scrutiny:

District 3 & Council President Hollingsworth Focus Several measures affecting District 3 and sponsored by Council President Joy Hollingsworth , who represents Central Seattle, are also queued up for Monday’s session:

Hollingsworth’s posture toward policing and City Hall security also drew pushback during Friday’s public testimony. One speaker criticized Hollingsworth’s policy requiring uniformed Seattle Police Department officers to staff Council Chambers during meetings which has added overtime costs to an understaffed department, arguing that criticism in chambers is protected free speech rather than a security threat.

Next Steps Monday’s meeting is accepting written public comment only and will follow a strict schedule including voting on the 16 pulled items, working through the 26-item individual-vote list including a compromised LEAD/CoLEAD evaluation request added Friday, considering Foster’s JumpStart carryforward amendment, and voting on standalone budget bills.
Strauss said he will not allow any new consent pulls and warned colleagues to prepare for an all-night marathon.

“I would expect to stay until we’re done on Monday. And that means all night,” Strauss said Friday evening, explaining that Central Staff needs Tuesday and Wednesday for technical quality control and balancing checks.

The committee will meet again on Thursday for final votes on the amended 2027 budget ordinance and 2028 endorsement resolution, sending the entire package to the full City Council for final passage on Friday, November 20th.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, November 16–22
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: (LITERATURE) Like many millennials, I grew up religiously watching LeVar Burton’s iconic educational PBS TV show Reading Rainbow , and it helped instill a love of reading in me early on. However, it wasn’t until watching the charming 2024 documentary Butterfly in the Sky: The Story of Reading Rainbow that I fully appreciated Burton’s cultural impact. Besides his work as a fierce literacy advocate, Burton also starred as main character Kunta Kinte in the groundbreaking 1977 ABC miniseries Roots and as Geordi La Forge in Star Trek: The Next Generation . He’s now telling his own remarkable story in his memoir Take My Word for It , which details his childhood during the Civil Rights Movement and his path to becoming an actor. Burton will join speaker, host, and cultural producer Kiesha B. Free, founder of the community resource directory Hey, Black Seattle!, for a conversation at Benaroya Hall. ( Benaroya Hall, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(FILM) Even as a die-hard Eric Rohmer lover, who believes he’s the second greatest French director of all time (Agnès Varda is obviously first), My Night at Maud’s was initially a hard sell for me. Firstly, because it’s about a Catholic engineer’s struggle with faith (snooze), and secondly, because it’s filmed in black and white, which is uncharacteristic for Rohmer’s typically color-drenched films. Little did I know, this film is far from a snooze, and even further from visually uninteresting. My Night at Maud’s is an unsung Christmas classic that takes place in the days leading up to Midnight Mass. There are glittering lights. There is a decorated tree. There are beautiful French people sulking about the holidays. What more could you ask for? ( SIFF Uptown, 7:30 pm ) AUDREY VANN

(MUSIC) Always All Ages: The Vera Project and Black Lodge are hosting a week of FREE shows and classes to celebrate 25 years of all-ages music, art, and community. Between the big names like AJJ, Deerhoof, Kimya Dawson and comedy by Chris Gethard and Demi Adejuyigbe, Friday and Saturday went quick, as free tickets do. Sometimes all-ages shows make me feel like a weird old guy with his arms crossed, but mostly they make me feel really glad that these resources are available to kids who are cooler than I was at that age anyhow. If you’re just finding out about these shows here in the newspaper, don’t fret, there will be very limited tickets available at the door—not to mention a banging local lineup on Wednesday Nov 18 featuring stand-outs Jackie Tulsa (whose 2026 album Good Year rules). ( Vera Project, 7 pm, free, all ages ) DYLAN BUECHE

(MUSIC) How lucky are we that Julien Baker chose Seattle for her three-night rock club residency tour. Just five cities made the cut: Salt Lake City, UT; Cambridge, MA; Carrboro, NC; Lawrence, KS; and Athens, GA. First the Seahawks win the Bad Bunny Super Bowl and now this? Mayor Katie Wilson’s Seattle really is where dreams come true! Baker may most commonly be known as one-third of boygenius, but she’s an incredible solo talent. Her songs, sometimes laden with sweeping piano and always packed with raw emotions, take hold of your heart and squeeze it until it starts to hurt and you start to squirm, but the squirming is where the healing happens. Judging from previous setlists, she seems to pull from the same pool of songs each night (good to know for anyone hoarding tickets to all three shows hoping for some kind of complete multi-day retrospective), but all Baker eras are there— Sprained Ankle , Turn Out the Lights (aka my depression’s personal soundtrack), and Little Oblivions —as well as yet-to-be-released tracks. Go ahead and skip your antidepressant for the day. Let Dr. Baker heal you. (Neumos, 7 pm, all ages) MEGAN SELING

(VISUAL ART) Tapestries made of AstroTurf and buckskin, blankets woven from ink and tape, a Cree prayer rendered in blood-red acrylic and powdery pastel: One of the year’s most anticipated shows (mine at least) opens this month at the Frye. An Indigenous Present is a traveling exhibition co-organized by the renowned artist Jeffrey Gibson and independent curator Jenelle Porter that includes major works and commissions by 15 Indigenous artists, spanning 100 years of Indigenous art. The exhibition embodies a shift in how Indigenous identity is represented within institutional spaces, as artists move beyond redefining their place within these institutions to actively defying the colonial constraints and expectations they have imposed for centuries. Alongside An Indigenous Present , the museum has mounted My Body Is a Basket , featuring work by three Indigenous Pacific Northwest artists—Brenda Mallory, Danielle Morsette, and Sara Siestreem—who push traditional basket weaving into unexpected conceptual and metaphorical territory. ( Frye Art Museum, 11 am-5 pm ) AMANDA MANITACH
A Musical Tribute to Fallen Hip-Hop Soldiers

(MUSIC) As a part of Diabetes Awareness month, Tisha Gallow, who certainly deserves the title The Queen of South Seattle, is presenting a tribute to rappers who passed away: Biggie Smalls, Phife Dawg, Eazy E, DMX, MCA, Tupac, and more. The show will involve live contributions by some of Seattle’s best players: Roc Phizzle, Rick Pitts, and Ngoma Numu. Vitamin D will be on the ones and twos. And you will be there to say, in the words of the late Guru, “I wish you were still living, in memory of….” Rest In Peace. ( Columbia City Theater, 8 pm, 21+ ) CHARLES MUDEDE

(MUSIC) For my fellow millennials who were raised by Nickelodeon and are activated like a sleeper agent by the words “Move it, football head!”: this one’s for us. Award-winning composer Jim Lang, known for scoring the Hey Arnold! series and its associated films, is bringing the beloved animated show’s music on the road in honor of its 30th anniversary (!), along with series creator Craig Bartlett and the official touring band, the PS 118 All Stars. Indulge in some ’90s nostalgia as you revisit the show’s greatest hits—by the way, did you know the cartoon’s fictional setting Hillwood, Washington is an amalgamation of Seattle, Portland, Brooklyn, and Chicago? That makes this a homecoming of sorts! ( Neptune Theatre, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

articles.title: Slog AM: Officials Say Ground Stop Wasn’t AI’s Fault, Longview Mill Had Problems Before Explosion, Old People Are Buying Teslas
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Ground town: The US airspace completely shut down on Friday, grounding flights nationwide. Delays and cancellations continued throughout the weekend. A communications network failure caused the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights out of an abundance of caution. Officials blame a new router in Arkansas flooding the system with new information after a system upgrade. This was part of an effort to replace copper wire with fiber optic cable.

It definitely wasn’t the FAA’s new AI, officials say . The $875 million SMART system the FAA just started rolling out to “predict problems in the sky” is not the culprit, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and the startup that designed the system. Pretty odd timing, though, you gotta admit!
Trump has finally spoken out about the ground stop: He has identified a new culprit. It’s Joe Biden, of course:

Microsoft products are functioning again: Hip, hip, hooray! Outlook is back. Microsoft said the outage that rendered several of its most critical products useless for over 24 hours last week was not a cyberattack and it was not related to AI. The outage was “an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” Microsoft told KUOW .

Trump goes to China: He’s meeting China’s leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in Shenzhen. This will be Trump’s first meeting with Xi this year without ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang usually attends these trips and has been central to shaping Trump’s views on the US’s technological competition with China. Trump says he doesn’t intend to bring the Nvidia situation up to Xi, including the allegations that a Chinese spy cavorted with Huang. He’ll leave that conversation up to Xi.
Vladimir Putin will also join this trip: It’ll be the first time Xi, Trump, and Putin have all met up together. Probably only good things can come from that meeting.

Meanwhile, in Huang World: After his resignation last week, new CEO Colette Kress is going to “ rein in ” some of the chipmaker’s deals. Nvidia had been functioning as a blank check for burgeoning AI companies. We’ll see how long that lasts; Huang may be flirting with a comeback as CEO.

Longview mill collapse could’ve been avoided: A new Seattle Times report looks into just how often Nippon Dynawave Packaging put off maintenance in the lead-up to the tank rupture that killed 11 workers earlier this year. Since 2019, the mill had “more than 30 spills, toxic releases, and chemical-related injuries.”

Cool, cool, cool: Israel has utilized the facial recognition platform run by Seattle’s neighborhood bookseller to analyze Palestinians. Israel uploaded 3.5 million pictures of Palestinians to Amazon’s AI-powered facial analysis platform Rekognition. In recent years, Israel has moved tons of data into Amazon’s data centers. This includes “sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation,” reports the Guardian .

Senior moment: Elderly Americans whose faculties have declined enough so they don’t drive themselves anymore are buying Teslas for the self-driving feature . That isn’t how it’s supposed to be used. Tesla’s self-driving feature requires supervision and human intervention if the system makes a mistake. Yet, Tesla isn’t advising against these new users; in fact, Tesla is supporting them and using testimonials from people who should not be behind any wheel as advertising. Car-dependence and lack of autonomy without an automobile is so very American. If only they knew about buses.
ICYMI: SNL got a little too real (compliment) in this sketch. Send it to your mom, aunt, or sister.

articles.title: Immigration enforcement continues to impact local families
articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: Six-year-old Victoria went to downtown Seattle earlier this year after being called in for an immigration court hearing. Officials had marked her as an “unaccompanied minor” - despite the fact she came to the U.S. with her parents - and separated her case from her parents’ case.
Advocates working closely with families told Cascade PBS they frequently see this process of separating kids' cases from their parents and believe it’s a tactic to sow confusion.

“In the last year we've really seen an escalation in the attacks by ICE on migrant families, migrant children, migrant women," said Anna Beyette, an organizer with International Women’s Alliance. “What we've actually seen, since the start of the year, is the escalation of particularly children's courts into something that they're referring to as ‘mega master’ hearings.”

Those hearings often saw dockets with a hundred cases or more per day. Beyette says the mega master hearings have slowed since this summer, but the number of cases in a regular court day has still gone up. She estimates that dockets had about a dozen cases a day before the mega master hearings began, and now they have an average of 50 60 cases in a regular court day.

In the first half of this year, more than 300 children were arrested as part of immigration enforcement in Washington. But that is only a fraction of the kids who have ongoing cases and could be called into court. Beyette estimates the number of children with hearings this year to be over a thousand.

“It's terrifying for the children. Many of them are young,” Beyette said. “When you go in there, you see families with babies and toddlers who are there for their toddlers' appointments. And so to ask children to advocate for themselves oftentimes in like not their native language, without proper information to them about what's happening, is just really a violation of their human rights.”
Many of those arrested are between 10 and 14 years old. But some arrests are for kids much younger, including a handful that were under a year old.

As for 6-year-old Victoria, Beyette and many others successfully rallied to push for her case to be reconnected to her mom’s case. She says she sees that as a win not just for Victoria, but for every family encountering this situation.

“One thing that I really want to make very clear is that even as there are these heightened attacks on migrant families and our communities, we're seeing people fighting back,” she said. “Even as they're afraid for their families, they're fighting back because migrants always are at the forefront of fighting not just for their families, but to end a system that is forcing them from their homelands and then targeting them when they come here to the U.S.”

• The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA

A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline.

The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.”

articles.title: Though Trump is giving him the cold shoulder, Netanyahu is pulling out all the stops to cling to power. And he just might | Simon Tisdall
articles.author: Simon Tisdall
paras: The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice

It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet h is final downfall remains far from certain.

As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary lengths to cling to power, using every dirty trick in his well-thumbed handbook while calling for a “government of national unity” (excluding Arab parties). And the perception he has been hung out to dry by a similarly electorally humbled Donald Trump , his biggest ally, may also prove over-optimistic. Besieged Palestinians in the West Bank and in hungry, flooded Gaza, and the bombed and battered people of Iran, have good reason to be fearful.
Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

articles.title: How the US elections and Iran war are influencing the UN’s COP31 climate talks – and discussions around fossil fuels
articles.author:
<name>Jennifer Morgan, Senior Fellow, Center for International Environment and Resource Policy and Climate Policy Lab, Tufts University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jennifer-morgan-2548101"/>
paras: The 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact. That’s evident as I listen to government officials and others from around the world at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

World leaders are seeing their countries suffer from intensifying storms and heat fueled by climate change and from one of the worst global energy crises in history. A U.N. report found that global warming will overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the level countries agreed a decade ago to try to avoid because of the growing risk of dangerous climate change.
The Middle East conflict has intensified oil and gas price and supply volatility , pushing economies to the brink as energy and food prices spike and energy security falters.
Countries that rely on imported fossil fuels for their energy sources have borne the brunt of the energy crisis. Those doubling down on renewable energy are weathering the crisis better.

In Pakistan, for example, the rapid expansion of solar power over the past six years helped the country avoid more than US$12 billion in fossil fuel imports before the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran began in February 2026. One forecast suggests solar could save the country more than $6 billion more by the end of the year. Spain, which relies less on natural gas and more on solar energy for electricity than most European countries, kept electricity prices lower and avoided the worst of the gas-driven spikes seen in more exposed systems such as Italy’s.

In formal negotiations and in meetings around the U.N.’s broader Global Climate Action Agenda , countries are working on ways to accelerate the use of clean energy and to provide poorer countries with the resources to adapt to climate change and expand clean energy.

I have been following international climate negotiations for years as a former special climate envoy for Germany and senior fellow at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. In 2026, after two years of the Trump administration’s pressure to get countries to abandon efforts to slow climate change , I’m seeing rising concern among leaders about the costs of fossil fuels on economies and people’s lives.

A step in transitioning away from fossil fuels is shifting to electrification powered by clean energy. The co-presidents of COP31, from Turkey and Australia, have proposed a global target of 35% of all energy use coming from electricity by 2035 – including for transportation and industry – and they are working to persuade other countries to sign on.

Hitting that 35% mark could save fossil-fuel-importing countries $400 billion a year , according to the International Energy Agency. In consumer terms, $100 spent on electricity powers a car up to three times farther than $100 of gasoline, based on global averages. Reaching the goal could slash energy emissions across transportation, buildings and industry by up to 55% by 2035 .

However, the source of electrification matters. Forecasts from the International Renewable Energy Agency show that at least 78% of the electricity powering the world must come from renewable energy sources to keep global warming under the 1.5 C limit. Electrification delivers for both the climate and energy security if it runs on clean power instead of energy from oil, gas and coal.
Getting the world to that point will require addressing some key barriers: the cost of infrastructure needed to deliver clean energy and the need for policies to encourage the changes.

Beyond the formal negotiations, countries are discussing multiple initiatives to provide technical support to one another , as countries develop power grids that can manage the variability of solar and wind power, and financial help to countries that need it.

The high financial and environmental costs of fossil fuels have been reshaping global politics. Voters came out in big numbers over the past few months to elect leaders who support clean, affordable energy solutions.
The world saw this notably with the reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the biggest Democratic congressional victory in the United States in over three decades.

Lula, in his first international trip after winning his fourth term, called on the COP31 presidents to carry forward Brazil’s work as host of COP30 on a transition away from fossil fuels . He announced that Brazil will host a future conference on the fossil fuel transition, following the first in Colombia in April 2026 and a second planned in 2027 in the island nation of Tuvalu.

Brazil has clearly emerged as a climate superpower in Antalya. With its greatest one-year reduction in deforestation and its leadership in producing three plans, known as road maps, to help the world transition away from fossil fuels, end deforestation and provide the $1.3 trillion in financing needed for developing countries, Brazil has demonstrated it understands the urgency of the climate crisis.
We will see whether the co-presidents of COP31 will answer the calls from Lula and U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to support these road maps becoming formal guidance for all countries.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a delegation of 18 members of the U.S. House of Representatives also came to COP31 to signal the presence of American leadership on future climate policy. President Donald Trump has pulled the U.S. out of the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement and dozens of other international organizations and treaties . The U.S. did not send a formal delegation to the climate talks.
As former U.S. climate envoy John Kerry said in Antalya , “Americans did vote for clean, affordable energy, and they also voted for clean governance.”

The international community will be watching to see whether the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress can help safeguard U.S. climate science after the Trump administration’s extensive funding cuts , and whether it will restore critical funding to international efforts dealing with climate change.

At COP31, the shift in the real-world politics of energy has dominated several events and the formal negotiations. But the countries that are likely to lose from such a transition are also working diligently to slow this transition . On the opening day, a coalition of oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia announced it opposed any mention of Brazil’s road map away from fossil fuels in the official COP31 agreement.

For COP31 to be a success, the diplomatic process must demonstrate that it can catch up to the real economy and meet this moment of energy and climate crisis. I believe the summit’s final agreement should accelerate the electrification of infrastructure around the world and, at the same time, drive the transition away from fossil fuels in order to protect global security, economic stability and everyday citizens.
