articles.title: New England’s first Bible, published in an Indigenous language, had one aim: Converting Native Americans
articles.author:
<name>Peter C. Mancall, Distinguished Professor and Professor of the Humanities, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/peter-c-mancall-313858"/>
paras: In 1663, colonial printers in New England produced a translation of the Bible into Wampanoag, an Algonquian language spoken in southern New England . Also known as Wôpanâak or Massachusett , it was one of several Native American languages in the region.
Printing the book would be an important story on its own. But it is even more remarkable because it was the first Bible that English colonists published in North America.

As a historian of early America , I believe this Bible sheds important light on relations between New England’s Native peoples and English immigrants, who saw themselves as crucial players in the spread of Protestant Christianity. Consumed with the idea that their culture was superior, many English Protestants believed they could conquer North America without much bloodshed : that Indigenous peoples would voluntarily abandon their cultures and embrace the faith of the newcomers.

The historical record is more complex. My 2026 book, “Contested Continent,” details the struggle to control North America in the generations after Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic Ocean. There were many moments, including the fabled first Thanksgiving of 1621 , when Indigenous peoples and colonists coexisted. But there was brutal violence as well , such as English colonists’ efforts to destroy the Pequot of southern New England in 1637.
In the aftermath of early warfare, some Puritan clerics looked for new ways to convert Native Americans – and decided religious texts were the answer.

During the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther argued that the only infallible source of religious understanding was the Bible , a doctrine known as “sola scriptura.” Protestants believed the laity needed to become literate, in order to read Scripture for themselves.

The Puritans embraced this teaching, and in 1638, the Rev. Joseph Glover paid to transport a printing press to Cambridge , Massachusetts. Two years later, that press published the Bay Psalm Book , a collection of songs for worship – the first book printed in English North America.

In the years that followed, printers offered many religious tracts , often based on sermons. They believed that print would bring Protestant Christianity to a widening audience and provide guidance for existing believers.

A Puritan minister named John Eliot sailed from England to Boston in 1631 and soon took a leading role in the church at Roxbury, just south of the city. Eliot was so devoted to books that he purportedly brought 23 barrels of them with him from England.

By the 1640s, he began trying to spread his faith among Native residents of the region. To do so, he needed to be able to communicate with those he hoped to convert, and he understood that books could advance his cause.

Other colonists also hoped that print could foster good relations with the Native residents of New England. The most famous was Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island. “ A Key into the Language of America ,” a book he published in London in 1643, provided phrases in Narragsansett , another Algonquian language. Such efforts were crucial to Europeans eager to trade with Native peoples – and to those, like Williams, who wanted to spread their culture without violence .

Eliot was intent on translating the Bible. He did not know Wampanoag, but he met an interpreter who impressed him: Cockenoe, a Montauk man from Long Island who had been taken captive during the Anglo-Pequot War in 1637. He became crucial to the Cambridge-educated cleric’s cause.

Eliot was unstinting in his praise of Cockenoe , whom he called a “pregnant witted young man.” He pronounced words clearly, which was crucial for Eliot: Like almost all Native languages in North America at the time, Wanpanoak did not have a writing system, so Eliot needed to transcribe what he heard.

Cockenoe’s instruction enabled Eliot to produce religious works in Wampanoag, including the Ten Commandments and the Lord’s Prayer. In 1663, printers Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson published “ Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God ,” Eliot and Cockenoe’s full translation of the Bible.

Their Bible included some lines in English so that a literate person could recite the Native words out loud to others, even if they did not know the meaning. Green ordered enough paper to produce 1,000 copies of the book, although it is difficult to know how many existed.

Cockenoe was not the only Indigenous resident who worked on the Bible. Wawaus , a Nipmuc man from what is now central Massachusetts , helped set type for the book. Also known as James Printer, he was studying at Harvard’s Indian College , which had been established in 1655 to spread Christianity among Native peoples.
Eliot’s efforts to convert Indigenous peoples extended beyond translation , giving him the sobriquet “apostle to the Indians.”

He also worked with a missionary society to establish new towns where Algonquian-speaking peoples would abandon their traditional practices and live like colonists. Residents were to halt seasonal migrations, which had been crucial to their economies, and instead live year-round in houses. They were to dress like colonists, follow colonial laws and embrace Protestant religious practices .

Meanwhile, the growth of the colonial population was putting added pressure on Indigenous peoples who lived nearby. By the mid-1670s, any remaining goodwill between many Indigenous peoples and English colonists faded in a contest over limited resources , which was particularly difficult for Native Americans not living in the missionary communities.

In 1675, tensions erupted into what was called Metacom’s or King Philip’s War , named after the Wampanoag leader who led a widespread rebellion against colonists. The two-year conflict spread across southern New England and reached the shores of Casco Bay in present-day Maine. According to historian Jill Lepore , it was the deadliest war in American history , in proportion to the population.

Among the victims were the Native converts in the towns Eliot helped to establish, including Natick , a community west of Boston. Colonial authorities rounded them up, transported them to an island in Boston harbor and sold many into slavery . Even those who escaped the ravages of war found themselves struggling to maintain their shrinking lands .
Eliot believed that literacy was crucial for spreading his faith. In Cockenoe he found a talented partner. But mastering literacy could be a double-edged sword.

In 1676, in the midst of Metacom’s War, soldiers came across a note in English in the smoldering ruins of Medfield, a colonial town destroyed by Native Americans. Possibly written by Wawaus, the brief message warned that Indigenous residents would fight for years to maintain their lands .

Some colonizers, including Eliot, hoped to avoid using guns and bloodshed to advance their faith. But their goal was still destruction: to eliminate Algonquian cultures. As Wawaus’ note and Algonquian-speaking peoples’ presence in New England today reveal, those efforts failed.
Peter C. Mancall has received funding for his research from the National Endowment for the Humanities, the Huntington Library, Oxford University, and the University of Southern California.

articles.title: US loses measles elimination status – an epidemiologist explains what it will take to regain it
articles.author:
<name>Katrine L. Wallace, Assistant Professor of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/katrine-l-wallace-2626740"/>
paras: The United States has lost its measles elimination status – an international designation reflecting an absence of local measles transmission for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held since 2000 . A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a formal announcement expected Nov. 17 .
Canada lost its measles elimination status in 2025 , as did the United Kingdom and other countries in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases and still circulates in much of the world . What keeps the disease in check is herd immunity – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s at least 95% . But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine .

I’m an epidemiologist who studies misinformation in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage that kept measles from spreading.

A measles vaccine has existed in the U.S. since 1963 . The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about 97% effective . A federal program created in 1993 made it free for eligible children . After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases dropped more than 99% , and by 2000 measles was declared eliminated .

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that maintaining elimination status would require sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.
So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

Before the vaccine , measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases .

About 1 in 20 children who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called immune amnesia , leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.
In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis , which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a child in Los Angeles died of it .

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted 5,412 cases for 2026 – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, 1 in 6 have been hospitalized .

Six deaths appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which now relies on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in Pennsylvania , one in New York and two in Wisconsin .

Pennsylvania’s outbreak alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. Major outbreaks have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. Utah’s outbreak , which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have triggered the loss of elimination status .
When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.

Parents who had never seen measles had nothing vivid to weigh against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper fraudulently linking MMR to autism was retracted in 2010 , and its author lost his medical license . But the damage was already done, and this myth persists to this day , even though studies that included millions of children have found no link .

During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine misinformation proliferated in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots has fallen every year since the 2019-20 school year.

In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines . Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of medical freedom to gain a larger, more mainstream audience .
Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.

On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for MMR to be split into three single-disease shots , which are not sold in the United States . There is no published evidence that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean more chances for missed doses .

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While questioning the vaccine and measles deaths, he has promoted vitamin A and nutrition as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a supportive treatment , not a cure or vaccine substitute.
Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26 . Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a record 4.2% .

Of this year’s cases, 96% were unvaccinated or of unknown status. The 92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with 75.2% among Idaho kindergartners , while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.
Adult immunity also has gaps : Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one.

Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least 12 months without continuous transmission . That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.
But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about.

The Department of Health and Human Services blames current vaccination gaps on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. CDC Director Erica Schwartz said that the agency would not make any changes in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status.
Additionally, orders like August’s about the MMR vaccine, and revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations , are weakening vaccination efforts .

Also, on top of a chronically underfunded public health infrastructure , many career public health scientists lost their jobs in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible has been substantially weakened .
So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever.

articles.title: Lucía Caminos is the first Latina ‘Grand Theft Auto’ lead – these video game characters paved the way
articles.author:
<name>Regina Marie Mills, Associate Professor of American Culture, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/regina-marie-mills-1380522"/>
paras: If the Netflix-exclusive trailer that briefly crashed the streaming service in August 2026 is any indication, “ Grand Theft Auto VI ” – a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style crime saga set in a satirical, fictionalized Florida – may be the most anticipated video game of all time .

It’s been 13 years since gaming company Rockstar released a new title in its flagship franchise. Fans have spent years dissecting leaked footage , constructing elaborate theories about the game’s mechanics and even attempting to reconstruct its fictional map using real-world geography .

But as a Latino studies scholar who teaches and researches video games , I’m most excited by the fact that “Grand Theft Auto VI” is the first title in the series to feature a Latina lead character: Lucía Caminos .
Not everyone is thrilled about a female protagonist – sexism, after all, remains a persistent issue in the gaming community.

But it nonetheless represents a watershed moment, as Latina video game characters have historically played second fiddle. Latino popular culture scholar Frederick Luis Aldama has pointed out how Latinos usually exist as obstacles for players to overcome rather than heroes whose stories players get to experience firsthand.

At the same time, a host of Latina characters throughout video game history – some playable, most not – paved the way for Lucía. Together, they show how representation is less about skin color and more about connection, complexity and character development.
In 1985, Carmen Sandiego was introduced as a criminal mastermind in “ Where in the World is Carmen Sandiego? ”
Players must pursue Carmen as she leaves a trail of clues across the globe. But Brøderbund, the game’s developer, left Carmen’s ethnic identity and origins ambiguous.

While researching the Brøderbund Collection at the Strong Museum of Play, I learned that the game’s creators originally imagined Carmen as a man named Estaban Devious who was born in Andorra, a tiny country in the Pyrenees with a large Spanish-speaking population. Brøderbund eventually settled on Carmen Sandiego – a name deemed exotic and befitting of a world traveler.

Despite Carmen’s unclear origins, Latinas have long connected with her. Actress Gina Rodriguez was so taken with Carmen as a kid that she jumped at the chance to voice Carmen in the animated series “ Carmen Sandiego ,” which premiered on Netflix in 2019 and ran for four seasons. According to Rodriguez , Carmen was “an incredible, strong, feminist, badass Latina who was going around the world. … I wanted to be just like her.” This cartoon gave Carmen a clear backstory – she was Argentine – and complicated her portrayal as a villain by having her turn on the very criminal organization she once belonged to.

With the show introducing Carmen Sandiego to a new generation of kids, new titles continue to appear . To coincide with Carmen’s 40th anniversary, “ Carmen Sandiego ” was released in 2025. It finally makes Carmen a playable character.
Like Carmen Sandiego, Isabela Keyes is a villain. One of the antagonists of the 2006 game “ Dead Rising ,” Isabela is the sister of Carlito Keyes, who initiates a zombie outbreak in Colorado.

Players discover that Isabela and Carlito infected people with the zombie virus to avenge the destruction of their hometown, Santa Cabeza, a fictional Central American village. The U.S. government had been experimenting with the virus there and destroyed the town to cover up its research.
But Isabela eventually realizes that she and Carlito have gone too far. She has a change of heart and ends up turning against her brother.

I think of Isabela as an important Latina video game character because she’s not simply included as a pretty face. That’s too often been the case for Latina characters, whether it’s Cynthia Velasquez in “Silent Hill 4” – whose alternate costume in the game made her look like a Playboy bunny – or Katarina Alves in “Tekken 7,” whose default and alternate costumes prominently feature her thong.

Capcom, the studio that produced the game, nonetheless marketed Isabela as a sex symbol. The question of how to interpret this sort of sexualization has divided gamers and scholars. On the one hand, many game designers still see their target audience as heterosexual men. However, women now make up half the gaming market , and overtly sexualized characters, which continue to appear, could further the sexism that bedevils the industry .
Video games have historically featured few queer characters , let alone queer Latino characters .

But indie games, which are developed outside major studios and often prioritize creative experimentation over commercial conventions, have generally been more welcoming to LGBTQ+ narratives and representation.

Fullbright’s 2013 exploration game “ Gone Home ” tells a 1990s coming-out story. Players explore the empty Oregon home of Katie Greenbriar and gradually learn the story of her younger sister, Sam, and Sam’s Mexican American girlfriend, Lonnie DeSoto, who hopes to one day join the military.

Though Lonnie is not a playable character, players piece together her experiences through letters and other clues. They learn about the challenges Lonnie faces as a Latina lesbian in the Junior Reserve Officers Training Corps, a high school program that teaches military-style leadership and discipline. By incorporating aspects of 1990s zine culture, the U.S. military’s Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell policy toward homosexuality and the feminist punk movement Riot Grrrl , “Gone Home” accurately and realistically captured the hopes and fears of being LGBTQ+ in the 1990s.

For years, playable Latina characters were pretty much nonexistent. Opportunities almost exclusively came from the large rosters of fighting games – characters like Ángel in the 2001 game “King of Fighters” and Christie Monteiro in “Tekken,” also released in 2001.
Over the past decade, that’s started to change.

Sombra is a Mexican hacker and one of the most prominent characters in the 2016 futuristic shooter “Overwatch.” Born Olivia Colomar, she was orphaned as a child and grew up in Mexico, where she developed extraordinary computer skills. She works with the game’s antagonists but pursues her own agenda of unraveling a global conspiracy.

Zyanya Mondragón , better known as Reyna, is a Mexican character in the 2020 futuristic shooter “VALORANT.” Reyna is a supernatural warrior who absorbs the life energy of enemies she kills, using it to heal herself and grow stronger. But her bloodthirsty nature has a deeply personal motivation: She needs the life energy she harvests to keep her younger sister, Lucia, alive.

These two characters have compelling pasts and aren’t clear-cut antagonists. However, they still sometimes fall victim to the “ sexy Latina ” stereotype. For example, in a segment of Conan O'Brien’s Clueless Gamer series, in which the blundering comedian tries out new video games, O'Brien repeatedly ogles over Sombra’s body .

Lucía Caminos will join just a handful of playable Latina characters, like Kait Diaz from “Gears of War,” in what are known as “ AAA games ” – titles with the biggest marketing and development budgets. But unlike the “Gears of War” franchise, which was Xbox-only on release, “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be released simultaneously on PlayStation 5, Xbox and the PC.

Yes, Lucía Caminos is an attractive young woman who breaks the law. But richly developed video game characters can move beyond stereotypes and give players new ways to imagine marginalized people as heroes. Rather than judging characters like Lucía as examples of either good or bad representation, it might be better to think about how players can reinterpret their stories, see them as role models and identify with their struggles.
After all, gamers have been doing just that since Carmen Sandiego.

articles.title: Rumi is one of America’s most popular poets – but translations often strip his poetry of its Islamic roots
articles.author:
<name>Peter Dziedzic, Ph.D. Candidate in Religious Studies, Harvard University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/peter-dziedzic-2710496"/>
paras: Every December, thousands of visitors gather in Konya, Turkey, to mark the death of the 13th-century poet Jalal al-Din Rumi. His followers call the night “ Shab-e ‘Arūs ,” the wedding night, and it is the moment they believe he was united with God.

Following Rumi’s death in 1273, his disciples formed the Mevlevi order , a Sufi brotherhood whose members are known in the West as the “whirling dervishes.” A dervish, from a Persian word for a poor person, is a member of a Sufi order who has committed to a life of spiritual discipline under a teacher. The Mevlevi order spread, and its lodges became centers of music and poetry. Mevlevi musicians helped shape Ottoman classical music , and the whirling dervish remains one of Turkey’s most recognizable cultural symbols today.

On the anniversary of Rumi’s death, white-robed dervishes perform a ceremony known as Sema . The ceremony opens with a hymn praising the Prophet Muhammad , followed by the sound of the “ney,” or reed flute. Accompanied by drums and chanted poetry, the dervishes then turn slowly around the hall, right palm raised to receive God’s blessing and left palm lowered to pass it on to others. For the Mevlevis, the whirling is not a performance but a form of worship, a remembrance of God carried out with the whole body.

In the United States, thousands of miles away, the same poet’s words appear on wedding programs, yoga studio walls and social media feeds. Rumi is one of the best-selling poets in the U.S. Despite this, many Americans may not know how deeply the Muslim legal scholar and preacher’s poetry is steeped in religion.

As a scholar of Sufism , the mystical tradition within Islam, I see a gap between these two Rumis – the Muslim mystic revered in Konya and the spiritual sage quoted on Instagram. The popular English translations that made Rumi famous strip the spiritual depth of his writing, which comes from his Islamic faith.

Rumi was born in 1207 in Balkh, in present-day Afghanistan. As armies of the Mongol empire – the largest contiguous land empire in history, which at its height stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe – advanced across Central Asia, his family moved west, eventually settling in Konya.

Like his father, the preacher Baha al-Din Walad, Rumi trained in Islamic law and theology and became a respected teacher. His life changed in 1244, when he met Shams of Tabriz, a wandering Sufi teacher. Their intense companionship upended Rumi’s scholarly life.

After Shams disappeared a few years later, Rumi poured his longing into thousands of lyric poems, later gathered as the Divan-e Shams . Most of these are ghazals: short love poems built on a single repeating rhyme, many of them composed during gatherings of music and dance.
Rumi’s masterpiece came later and took a different form – the “masnavi.”
A “masnavi” is a type of Persian poetic form built from rhyming couplets.

The two lines of each couplet rhyme with each other, and the next couplet can switch to a new rhyme. Because the poet never has to sustain a single rhyme across the whole poem, the form can run on almost indefinitely, which made it a favored vehicle for long poems. Other Sufi poets used it to compose spiritual epics.

Rumi’s own “Masnavi-ye Ma'navi,” or “Spiritual Couplets,” better known as “the Masnavi,” is one of the genre’s most celebrated examples. At the urging of his disciple Husam al-Din Chelebi, Rumi began dictating it around 1258 and continued until his death, producing some 25,000 couplets across six books.

Rumi’s “Masnavi” opens with the song of a reed flute lamenting its separation from the reed bed, an enduring Sufi metaphor of the soul longing to return to its divine source. What follows is less a single story than a vast, winding conversation that includes animal fables, bawdy tales, Quranic stories and reflections on the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad and those who came before him.

Rumi held his “Masnavi” in high regard. In the Arabic preface to its first book, he described it as “ the roots of the roots of the roots of religion ” and “the explainer of the Quran.” That is a bold claim, but it reflects how the poem works. Its couplets are threaded with Quranic verses, often quoted in the original Arabic, which Rumi then unfolds through stories and images to draw out their deeper meanings.

Later admirers went further. A famous Persian verse calls Rumi’s Masnavi “ the Quran in the Persian tongue ,” a line traditionally attributed to the 15th-century poet Jami. For centuries, Muslims from the Balkans to South Asia have gathered in circles to read and study the “Masnavi” line by line.

Translating any poem involves trade-offs – between sound and sense, between keeping the original’s rhyme and meter and capturing its meaning, and between staying close to the text and making it feel natural to a new audience. With Rumi, the stakes are especially high because so much of his meaning lives in the religious world his poems draw on. Faithful translations exist, but they are not the ones most Americans read.
Scholars such as Reynold Nicholson produced careful English translations of Rumi in the early 20th century, but the versions most Americans know are something different.

The most popular are by the American poet Coleman Barks , whose books popularized Rumi from the 1970s onward. Barks did not read Persian . Instead, he reworked earlier scholarly translations into free-verse American English, a process Duke University scholar Omid Safi calls “a double translation.”

Jawid Mojaddedi , who translated the “Masnavi” starting in 2004, told The New Yorker : “The Rumi that people love is very beautiful in English, and the price you pay is to cut the culture and religion.”
References to the Quran, the Prophet and Muslim ritual are often softened or dropped. Where Rumi writes “God,” Barks sometimes substitutes “the Beloved.”

Take one of Barks’ best-loved lines – “There are hundreds of ways to kneel and kiss the ground.” As Safi points out, Rumi’s Persian refers to “ruku” and “sujud,” the bowing and prostration of the Muslim ritual prayer performed five times a day. The English is lovely, but it turns a specific Muslim act of worship into a general image of reverence.

Or consider one of Rumi’s most quoted lines in English – “Out beyond ideas of wrongdoing and rightdoing, there is a field. I’ll meet you there.” A closer rendering of the Persian reads: “Beyond Islam and unbelief, there is a desert plain.”

In other words, Rumi is not dismissing faith or morality. He is making a classic Sufi claim that the deepest love of God lies beyond the labels people use to sort believers from unbelievers. That is a striking thing for a Muslim jurist and preacher to say, and it carries its full force only when the reader knows who is saying it. The popular version turns it into generic advice about not judging others.
These are not isolated choices. Across the popular versions, the world Rumi lived in — the Quran he quoted, the prayers he performed, the prophets whose stories he retold — is largely absent.

It might be tempting to treat all this as a debate for specialists, but for millions of Americans, Rumi is one of the few Muslim voices they have ever read. How he is translated shapes how they understand not only the poet, but the tradition he came from.

Safi has described the erasure of Islam from these New Age versions as “ spiritual colonialism ,” a process of bypassing and erasing a spiritual landscape that has been lived and breathed by Muslims across the world. Western readers embrace the beauty of Rumi’s poetry while setting aside the faith that produced it and the communities that have treasured it for centuries.

None of this means Americans should stop reading Rumi in English. Barks and others have introduced millions of people to a poet they might never have encountered. Additionally, newer verse translations of the “Masnavi,” such as Mojaddedi’s six-volume edition , try to carry over both its form and its Islamic framework.
The larger task is to read Rumi as Muslims from Turkey and Iran to Afghanistan and South Asia have read him for centuries – as a poet whose expansive vision grew out of his faith, not in spite of it.

At a time when Muslims are often cast as outsiders in American public life, presenting one of the world’s most beloved poets as spiritual in spite of Islam, rather than because of it, reinforces a damaging story.
Peter Dziedzic received a funded fellowship from the American Council of Learned Societies in 2026.

articles.title: Annual water-quality reports don’t tell the full story of what you’re drinking
articles.author:
<name>Sarah Glass, Ph.D. Candidate in Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice Water Institute, Rice University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sarah-glass-2545173"/>
paras: Water is vital to life, which is part of why we study what’s in it.

Drinking water isn’t just H₂O – though there are over 15 septillion molecules of it in a standard glass. It also contains natural minerals, dissolved organic and biological matter, and substances that enter from agriculture, industry, consumer products and water treatment.

Most of these substances are harmless at the concentrations typically found in water. Some are beneficial, and even essential , such as sodium, fluoride and calcium ions, which build strong bones and teeth. Additionally, these ions balance electrolytes that regulate bodily function.

In fact, drinking large quantities of completely demineralized or distilled water can disrupt the body’s electrolyte balance. This water would dilute the natural sodium levels in blood, potentially causing hyponatremia , a condition with symptoms such as nausea, headache, confusion and seizures.

Most people encounter water-quality science through an annual report from their local water company . It’s usually a couple of pages long with chemical names and numbers in a table. It lists various compounds that may exist in the water, summarizes what has been found in tests of the water source, and explains whether the water meets government-set standards that promote and protect public health and safety .
These reports provide important information about drinking water safety, but they are not a complete inventory of every substance scientists can detect or are working to understand.

We study a range of contaminants, chemical and biological, that are found in drinking water, with the goal of developing technologies to further safeguard public health. This includes pollutants and pathogens that are not included on an annual water report.

Consider perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, more commonly known as PFAS and also called “forever chemicals” because they persist in the environment for a long time. These are a large family of chemicals used in consumer products because they resist water, oil and heat.
Research has linked exposure to certain PFAS with adverse chronic health effects , such as endocrine disruption, low birth weight in fetuses and certain types of cancer.

Federal drinking water standards now limit the amount of two common types of PFAS found in the environment to 4 parts per trillion, a level extremely hard to detect even on advanced analytical equipment. However, the broader chemical family includes many others whose occurrence and health effects are less understood by scientists and completely missed by the public or policy.

The challenge that water-quality engineers face is not simply to determine whether PFAS, or other compounds and pollutants, are present. Rather, researchers need to understand the concentrations of those chemicals in the water, how people are exposed to them, what their effects on the body are, and how effectively different treatment technologies can remove or destroy them.

Pharmaceutical residues from medicine that passes through people’s bodies enter sewage systems. Agricultural chemicals such as pesticides flow off croplands into waterways. Both of these types of waste can break down into new, less studied compounds as they move through soil and water, eventually collecting in groundwater or wastewater to be treated and redistributed. The potential long-term effects of these lesser-studied compounds are not fully understood.

Water treatment plants often use chlorine as part of the disinfection process. But when chlorine reacts with natural organic matter, such as decayed plants and microorganisms, it forms disinfection byproducts . These byproducts include chemicals such as trihalomethanes, which are known carcinogens that must be removed with further treatment before the water is safe to drink.

Some contaminants pose an immediate threat; others pose threats that accumulate over time. For instance, ingesting microplastics in drinking water may not hurt you right now, but they are being detected in people’s blood years after exposure. We water-quality scientists want to know not only what’s in the water, but what it might do to your body right away or across decades.

The timescale and route of exposure of waterborne contaminants matter, too. If stagnant pipes are left unused for a long time, bacteria can build up. Then, when people start a shower or an outdoor fountain, that bacteria travels into the air in mist. This poses a different kind of threat than exposure to a chemical pollutant in drinking water because this would lead to bacteria infection.

For example, when there is a large buildup of Legionella spp. , a group of bacteria that can grow in drinking water distribution systems and power plant cooling towers when condensation pools, people who inhale the water vapor can develop Legionnaires’ disease, an acute form of pneumonia. Waterborne pathogens and their associated infections account for billions of dollars in maintenance and healthcare costs annually.

Moreover, it is important to distinguish what is hazardous and how it could eventually become a human health risk. In the case of Flint, Michigan , lead in a water pipe is a hazard, but as long as the water flowing through it is chemically stable and doesn’t react with lead from the pipes , the immediate risk to human health is low.

In the city’s 2014 water crisis, water from a new source was not chemically treated to reduce its ability to pick up lead from the pipes. By 2016, people had been ordered not to drink the water anymore because it was contaminated with dangerous levels of lead, which can cause neurological problems and impair brain function .

The real questions go beyond just looking at what’s in water, to include what kinds of dangers are there, whether immediate like Legionnaires’ disease or chronic like lead poisoning or cancer. Regulatory standards don’t always address every potential source or type of contamination.
The next time you review your local water report, don’t just look at what is being monitored; consider what may not be on the list at all.

articles.title: Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported . The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.
ULA said it doesn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it will work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.
The anomaly came about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn, according to Spaceflight Now. The Centaur is powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris.

Spaceflight Now also reported that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t identified the cause.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission . Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.
Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion , and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.
Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported .
ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin , and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.
Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Drops Design Director
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Michael Eliason, Director of Design & Policy at the Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD), departed that role last month in a personnel move that signals a strategic pivot for a public development authority still finding its footing. Eliason's former position will no longer exist, with the SSHD instead planning to hire a Director of Policy with a different portfolio of work.

Seattle voters created the social housing developer in 2023 by initiative, providing a mandate for the production of mixed-income, permanently affordable housing, operating independently of Seattle City Council or mayoral control. Two years later, voters approved a dedicated funding source for social housing via a high-earners payroll tax , with early revenue dramatically exceeding expectations in a way that has given the SSHD significant forward momentum .

Eliason had been brought on in January, after being closely involved in advocacy around Seattle's two social housing initiatives. Prior to becoming staff, he had served as one of the developer's first board members, an appointment made via members of Seattle's Green New Deal Oversight Board. Eliason's influence was credited with mandates for Passivhaus design being incorporated into the developer's mission from the jump.

Passivhaus standards create buildings that are highly energy efficient, using thermal insulation, airtightness, and filtered ventilation. While more expensive at the outset, the design creates cost savings as energy costs are reduced, with a benefit of providing more comfortable interior spaces that are more climate-friendly at the same time.

As a strong evangelist for Passivhaus standards and improved urban design, Eliason has pushed for green building requirements for social housing as a contributor for The Urbanist as well as in a book titled Building for People .

Eliason exited the developer just as it has appeared to hit its stride, announcing its first new construction project in the Central District and its second building acquisition in Delridge in the span of just a few weeks. After the SSHD board replaced its initial pick for CEO, Roberto Jimenez, with Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy – who had led the push for social housing in Seattle as co-founder of the advocacy group House Our Neighbors – things appeared to fall into place.
More social housing projects are expected to be announced soon, with a goal of owning 1,000 units by the end of 2027 and putting more in the construction pipeline.
In a post on LinkedIn made shortly after his departure, Eliason characterized the decision as a pivot away from an emphasis on design in future social housing buildings in Seattle.

"I recently learned that design would no longer be a priority for the Seattle Social Housing Developer, as they eliminated the Director of Design & Policy position," Eliason wrote. "It was an exciting run, and I am proud of the work I accomplished with the nearly three-year effort on the board, and then transitioning to staff. This work included massive efforts around standing up the real estate committee and working on the strategic plan - to finding viable and high quality parcels (not on arterials!), steering procurement efforts with architecture firms, working on legislative and local land use policies to deliver more/better/cost effective housing, and adding new construction values - all of which would go on to inform the design standards for new housing."

But sources familiar with how operations at the developer have disputed his characterization, instead pointing to a shift that has occurred as the SSHD has been navigating rules around public procurement for construction projects. Earlier this year, the SSHD rolled out a roster of design firms that will be considered for future developments, including CAST Architecture, Neiman Taber, Mithun, Schemata Workshop, and Perkins Eastman.

With those firms handling the bulk of design work, the SSHD does have less of a need for in-house design expertise, but did recently bring on Jacqui Aiello, former architectural designer at SMR Architecture, a firm focused on affordable housing. Aiello's hire could cut against the assertion that the developer is de-prioritizing design work.

"The Seattle Social Housing Developer made a sincere effort to keep Michael Eliason on staff by providing him with several options," SSHD Director of Communications Lilly Ana Fowler told The Urbanist. "We wish him the best with future endeavors and sincerely thank him for all his contributions to social housing. SSHD takes design seriously and is working with a number of architecture firms on both small and large social housing projects that prioritize family-sized housing, Passive House standards, open spaces and Universal Design."
Eliason did not respond to a request for comment from The Urbanist for this story.

The new Director of Policy position will be tasked with advocating for legislative changes to make it easier to build social housing in Seattle, and with representing the developer in front of governmental authorities, including the Seattle City Council. Rather than leading the design team, the role will be focused on translating "technical legal and regulatory ideas into clear, compelling information for audiences ranging from elected officials and agency staff to community members, the Board, and the media," according to a job posting from this month.

articles.title: Alternative Transit Modes
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained in an earlier guideway post, Sound Transit chose light rail technology to make it easier to use the existing transit tunnel and to run and stop at grade but many new technologies have been developed since. As Sound Transit builds a lot more elevated and tunneled sections and opens new lines in urban areas, it may need to reevaluate that decision. Sound Transit and Metro already use buses, heavy rail (for Sounder), ferries, and trams. Other cities like San Francisco, Mexico, and Paris use even more different modes like people movers and gondolas. In that post I talked about monorail and maglev guiderail systems. They are easier and faster to build due to prefabricated guideways, are slicker and therefore visually less obtrusive, and may offer easier maintenance.

As Sound Transit is facing escalating construction costs and feels it cannot accommodate traditional elevated trains downtown, it may be a good time to evaluate these and other alternative transit modes. Monorail systems have opened in Bangkok, and TSB has built a maglev test line in China and is looking at several options in Germany. Swyft Cities (working with Whoosh Solutions) and Ottobahn are working on cabins which hang from a guideway like the Wuppertaler Schwebebahn and provide personal rapid transit (PRT).

Similar to a Waymo or Zoox robotaxi, Swyft Cities and Ottobahn offer more route flexibility, are called via phone app, and have small individual cabins with an electric motor. Unlike a robotaxi, they use airspace and don’t get stuck in traffic, they are confined to its track network, have specific parking/staging areas, use electric motors with track power, and use small stations. While Swyft cabins travel on fixed cables (similar to a gondola or the RopeTaxi but those are propelled by the cable), Ottobahn cabins travel on regular tracks at 37mph. For longer distances Ottobahn claims up to 150mph. Both use track switches to guide cabins to their destination.

Ottobahn cabins hang off a bogie which is powered by an electric motor with regular wheels and steel tracks. Cabins either stop at elevated stations or can employ a lift mechanism which drops the cabin to the sidewalk for on- and off-boarding. Ottobahn claims they can support 6000 riders per hour in each direction, or even more with a favorable network design. Similar to a monorail, their track is supported by towers about 120ft apart and between 15 and 30ft high. The track can also cross longer distances over rivers and other obstacles akin to a suspension bridge. Cabins can usually climb up to 7%, with extra support even 12%. That may allow a ship canal crossing.
Swyft is hoping to start projects in Queenstown, Miami, or Los Angeles. Ottobahn started construction of its first network in Phuket .

Traditional train lines serve stations along a linear corridor. Turning a train around at the end of the line takes time as the operator usually has to switch from one end of the train to the other. Lines may branch towards the outer area of a network, but that splits the headway on each branch. As automated train systems do not need to worry about a driver, they can switch direction more easily and offer a bit more flexibility. For example, they can serve short stub lines by backing in and out, though that may impact travel time. PRT systems are not bound to any fixed line/schedule, can use a more elaborate track network, branch on demand, skip stations, and only stop as necessary. Though each cabin may be smaller, short headways may still allow for sufficient capacity.

Any of these systems promise simpler/faster guideway and station construction, easier integration into the existing urban infrastructure, more flexible branching capabilities, and more convenience for riders. It may be worthwhile to consider them for West Seattle or Ballard and other future lines.

articles.title: Seattle Street Ends: Eastlake
articles.author: John Feit (Guest Contributor)
paras: Today we will visit eight street ends and one park in the Eastlake neighborhood. In previous posts, we have looked at street ends around West Seattle , South Ship Canal , from Ballard to Fremont , from Fremont to Portage Bay , as well as the Duwamish Waterway . The last post was for South Lake Union's street ends .

For those new to this series, a little background on Seattle’s Shoreline Street Ends is helpful. Because Seattle is bounded and divided by numerous fresh and salt bodies of water the city has what are called ‘street ends’ — streets that end when they encounter a water body often continue under the water, sometimes resulting in mini-parks or recreational spaces. There are hundreds of such occurrences – almost as many as there are east-west and north-south streets.
Many of them, 142 to be exact, are part of a Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) program called Shoreline Street Ends. The program’s goals are to:

A little over half of the 142 street ends are defined by SDOT as “worth a visit,” while the remainder are either “not yet ready for visitors” or have “no public access.” Street ends are concentrated along the Ship Canal and Lake Washington, but also occur along each of the city’s other shorelines. Working with the city and neighborhoods to secure funding, pass legislation, and organize work parties, the non-profit and all-volunteer Friends of Street Ends help ensure Seattle’s accessible street ends grow in number and those already serving visitors continue to thrive.

Shoreline Street Ends vary in character from sandy beaches to docks wedged amongst shipyards and industrial uses. They are spacious and they are compact, and most are very easy to find. They support habitat for native species of flora and fauna and are convenient places to launch a kayak, sailboat, or motorboat. Oftentimes, they are adjacent to waterfront parks, expanding upon those assets. They are as varied as Seattle’s topography, and you can visit them any time.
Cycling is the best way to visit Seattle’s shoreline street ends. Many are accessed from low-traffic streets or bike paths.

Sitting beneath the Interstate 5 Ship Canal Bridge is the Furman Street street end. A fairly simple affair, it has a broad grass lawn leading to the water and a view towards the University of Washington campus and the several new highrises emerging in its neighborhood. Along Fuhrman and next to the street end is a rowing club, adding a nice buzz of activity.

WSDOT has closed the area off between the rowing club and the street end due to some hazards associated with falling debris from the underside of the bridge while it undergoes repairs. This condition will remain for some time until all necessary repairs are made. That being said it’s still worth a peek.

Partly sandy beach and partly forested landscape, the Martin Street street end can appear mysterious when viewed from Fairview Avenue due to its dense tree canopy and deep shadows. Probing beyond the shadows, however, one can find a waterfront bathed in sunlight. When I visited I happened upon a festive gathering that expanded my appreciation of street ends to be about more than water access and places to catch a view of the water to include unique social and gathering places. Residents from recent apartment development in the neighborhood have added new energy to what used to be a more isolated street end.
SDOT recently finished $375,000 in improvements (most done after these photos were taken). Even if you’ve previously visited the street end, here is a good reason to go again.

The most improved of Eastlake’s street ends, and among the most improved of those I have visited, is the East Allison Street street end. Although lacking the shelter and intimacy of East Martin Street, its staging area for watercraft, generous steps leading to the shoreline, and ADA accessible parking, make it very user friendly.
Right across from the street end is a new neighborhood corner coffee shop, adding a nice amenity to an otherwise desirable location.

East Hamlin Street combines many of the endearing features of Seattle’s street ends, albeit in rustic packaging. It provides a fantastic prospect for viewing Gas Works Park and an intimate lagoon with a sandy shoreline. Other amenities include park benches, a picnic table, as well as an ever changing assortment of lawn chairs along the waterline. The plantings include rose bushes, seagrasses, and a variety of other flora I’m ill equipped to identify. I especially liked the large deciduous trees hovering along its northern edge, their hues changing to golden in the fall day’s crisp air.

Things have been a little tidied up since I took these photos. The paths have new gravel and the benches were repaired, and the neighborhood stewards have done a great job improving and keeping the plantings looking great.

South of East Hamlin Street is East Edgar Street. Although not (yet) part of the Street End program, the Seattle Parks Foundation has information on potential improvements that you can learn more about.

Situated at the tail end of one of Eastlake’s few east-west arterials, Roanoke Street can be hard to miss despite its strategic location and generous amenities. If one looks beyond the parking area along its eastern edge, one finds new street furniture and a paved plaza.

Just to the north is a densely packed, and very urban collection of houseboats. Unlike other neighboring houseboat communities, those along Mallard Cove are arranged parallel to the shoreline giving them a density different from neighboring houseboat communities. This effect is further enhanced by the hillside buildings’ eastern edge.
Boeing’s first factory was located at the foot of Roanoke street.

Unique among the dozens of street ends I visited in the past, Louisa Street has a bocce court and a color theme, whose red brilliance was enhanced by the crimson trees hovering above its like-colored furniture when I visited in the fall.

Neighbors are calling it the Louisa Street Beach since children are having fun playing games in the sand. The two trees to the north have mulch and edging to keep users off the tree roots and we will do additional planting this Fall. This park gets lots of kayak use - a self-service rental is across the street. It also generally has someone simply sitting there and enjoying the day—in all kinds of weather.

Lynn Street Mini Park has a range of amenities and terrific views. Its sandy shoreline is a favorite launching spot for kayakers, and its generously furnished street level terrace allows one to glance above the water enthusiasts to Lake Union. Framed by houseboats to the south and a rare over the water condominium to the north, the park provides one of the more unique and beloved edges along the lake. Although not part of SDOT’s Street End program, and officially a Seattle City Park, its designation matters not for appreciating its fine qualities.

The East Boston Street street end is easily missed unless one has a map in hand. The street end itself is really just the sidewalk along Fairview Avenue – there is no access to the water. Instead, and if one picks just the right viewing angle to snatch a view between the heavily vegetated shoreline one is surprised to see a picturesque assembly of houseboats framing a view across the lake to Queen Anne.

East Newton Street, also known as Terry Pettus Park , is currently undergoing renovation. Prior to its being closed I was able to visit it on a fine fall day in 2023. This particular street end, at least prior to its renovation, had that rarest of amenities: a dock. The dock not only allows one a different way to access the water but it also provides a view back to the shoreline.

It is hard to pick a favorite among the many great street ends along Eastlake Avenue, but Newton Street would certainly be a contender. All construction permits for the renovation have been obtained and I’m sure the neighborhood eagerly awaits its reopening. Click here for project updates.

articles.title: Shoreline Pedestrian Bridge Defect Jeopardizes Already Delayed Timeline
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Any remaining hope of Shoreline opening its new pedestrian bridge over I-5 this winter appear dashed, after the project ran into a snag this month. KIRO reporter Chris Sullivan broke the news on Tuesday, noting builders were delaying the bridge placement that had been slated for November.

“Unfortunately, the contractor has discovered some manufacturing issues with one of the arches,” a City spokesperson told KIRO . “They are currently working with the manufacturer to resolve the issue. At this point, it is unclear if the manufacturer will be able to make corrections on site with the existing arch or if they will have to make a whole new arch. It will be another couple of weeks before they know for sure, and we have a new timeline.”

While Shoreline and its contractor, Kraemer North America, are still determining the extent of the issue, the City is framing it as a minor setback, with a spring 2027 opening still feasible. In fact, the City's project website portrays a spring 2027 opening as essentially the plan all along.

However, that would represent a significant delay from initial plans. In 2020, The Urbanist reported Shoreline was still hoping to open the pedestrian bridge close to concurrently with the light rail station. Lining up funding added planning delays, but an early 2026 opening had still been targeted once the project's $40 million budget had been assembled in 2024 , as Urbanist coverage noted at the time.

"While the project was in design we developed an early 2026 opening estimate. Securing final approvals to advertise for construction bids took longer than we anticipated, delaying that step by several months," Shoreline spokesperson Tavia Tan told The Urbanis t. "We advertised for bids in December 2024. Once the contractor joined the project, we updated the schedule based on the bridge manufacturer’s production timeline and input from the construction team. Those factors led to an estimate of 'early 2027' for the full bridge opening. Earlier this fall, we revised that projection to spring of 2027, primarily due to delays in procuring materials. This revision occurred before we identified the manufacturing issue."

Shoreline's two light rail stations opened on August 30, 2024, along with the rest of the Lynnwood Link extension . While the City had hoped to open the bridge as close to possible as light rail's arrival, it could end up being close to three years after the fact.

Once the pedestrian bridge is in place, residents in the rapidly densifying neighborhood to the west of I-5, which Shoreline rezoned in 2016 , will have direct access to South Shoreline Station without having to head down to the busy overpass at 145th Street – a street that is being supercharged with highway-style roundabouts.

If plans to place the bridge span this month had gone forward, the project still had other hurdles to clear before it could have opened, including completing a direct ramp to the light rail station platform and a trail connection on the west side linking people walking, rolling, and biking to 1st Avenue NE, a corridor which has been among the focal points of midrise development in the area.
The contractor plans to move forward with the trail work while the bridge span issue is being rectified.

"The original construction schedule called for placing the bridge span before building the connecting trail to 1st Avenue NE," Tan said. "The contractor has rearranged the work and is now building the trail. This flexibility allows construction to continue and helps limit delays while we determine the next steps for the bridge."

Sullivan noted a brief night-time freeway closure will be necessary once the bridge span is ready for installation: "You have likely seen the massive structure being built along the west side of the freeway for months. Shoreline had targeted Saturday, Nov. 7, or Saturday, Nov. 14, as the nights to close I-5 and lift the bridge into place. That installation has been delayed, but other work on the project is continuing."

Despite the lack of a pedestrian bridge, both of Shoreline's stations have been success stories, generating robust homebuilding activity and solid initial ridership numbers . Shoreline South averaged more than 3,600 daily boardings in October, boosted by a bus restructure that truncated Sound Transit's Route 522 bus at the station.

Shoreline North hovered around 2,800 daily boardings in September and October. Overall, the 1 Line corridor amassed just over 155,000 daily boardings in October, making it the busiest light rail system in the United States.
The addition of Shoreline's pedestrian bridge and continued residential growth offer a potent combination to build on that momentum.

articles.title: Five More Washington Cities Selected for State Growth Plan Reviews in 2027
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Washington's Commerce Department has released a list of five cities and towns that will see their housing growth plans subjected to additional state scrutiny next year, the second set of reviews planned under the 2025 Housing Accountability Act . Burlington, Friday Harbor, Mount Vernon, Oak Harbor, and Washougal will go under the microscope, with city leaders given deadlines to make any updates to their local Comprehensive Plans with the goal of ensuring that development regulations intended to pave the way for more diverse housing types across a range of income levels are in place.

The 2027 cities are mostly clustered around the north end of Puget Sound, in counties that had a state-mandated December 31, 2025 deadline to overhaul their local Comprehensive Plans. All five cities faced that deadline and didn't meet it, either leaving Commerce out of the loop when it comes to updating their plan or submitting a draft plan that the state found to fall short in some way.

The Housing Accountability Act represents something of a sea change in local housing growth planning that cities are still getting used to. Prior to its implementation, the only way to challenge a Comprehensive Plan that looked to be out-of-compliance with state law was to file a challenge at the state's Growth Management Hearings Board, a case-by-case appeal process that usually fell on private groups like neighborhood organizations or the statewide land use advocacy non-profit Futurewise to pursue.

Though the Commerce Department is often tasked with providing recommendations on local development standards and zoning changes, there wasn't a mechanism available to hold cities and towns that went too far their own way accountable. With the Housing Accountability Act, cities and towns are given a compliance deadline to make essential changes and if those aren't enacted, the so-called Builder's Remedy goes into effect – with local permit departments unable to deny building permits for residential projects that meet certain affordability requirements, regardless of the underlying zoning. Theoretically, that could mean skyscrapers in areas of the city that aren't used to dense housing.

Commerce is still in the middle of its 2026 "selected review" process, with zoning changes already adopted in three of the eight jurisdictions that made the list this year. So far, only Carnation has gotten to the stage of approving a final plan that is still being reviewed by Commerce, with Bainbridge Island and the 300-resident town of Beaux Arts Village both adopting interim regulations that provide additional time to adopt permanent changes down the road.

Next week, the City of DuPont, tucked into South Pierce County near Joint Base Lewis-McChord, is poised to be the first city to actually trigger the Builder's Remedy. Despite a timeline that doesn't call for adoption of potential changes to the city's Comprehensive Plan until early next year, DuPont has not requested an extension from Commerce that would prevent the Builder's Remedy from taking effect.

Though many of the jurisdictions that have been subjected to review so far have been relatively small, the impact is adding up. By the end of the second year, Commerce is on track to have reviewed cities and towns accounting for approximately 144,000 residents, more people than live in Washington's sixth largest city of Kent.

In turning its attention to Friday Harbor, Commerce will be jumping into the fray when it comes to one of the state's thorniest housing crises. As a tourist-oriented city with a high rate of seasonal housing, housing in Friday Harbor is regularly out-of-reach of the workers that the local economy relies on. Housing prices within San Juan County rose more than 100% between 2016 and 2022, far faster than median wages could ever compete with.

Despite increased demand for units in Friday Harbor, projects proposed in the city often turn highly contentious. Last year, a 49-unit development near Friday Harbor elementary school drew significant opposition, despite the inclusion of eight units of workforce housing in the project. The concerns raised included increased traffic, traffic safety impacts, and a lack of overall infrastructure, but the common denominator was the idea that Friday Harbor can't handle more population density.

Amanda Lynn, Executive Director of the San Juan Community Home Trust, offered an overall view of housing growth on San Juan Island, in an interview with the The Journal of the San Juans about that specific project.

“Every time you add a housing unit on this island, that requires infrastructure, that requires community resources like fire, police, school, anything you can think of,” Lynn said. “Every housing unit requires these things. So there’s always a balance beyond even just thinking about the ecosystem balance of the island itself.”
That balancing act, while clearly necessary in some regard on a ferry-dependent island, often means that lower-income residents trying to find homes in San Juan Island get the short end of the stick.

A state review under the Housing Accountability Act won't be able to fully solve Friday Harbor's housing crisis, of course. But it will likely ensure that barriers that stand in the way of housing production that aren't aligned with state law don't stay in place, adding clear repercussions if they do.

As these reviews continue to ramp up, pushback from local elected officials is another thing to watch for. As Beaux Arts Village councilmembers took their vote on interim development regulations last month, they also vowed to push for legislative changes that would modify the Housing Accountability Act to be less impactful on them. So far, what exactly it would look like to water down the legislation hasn't become clear, but as larger cities start to get subjected to that review, the political pressure could ramp up.

For now, however, the Housing Accountability Act does appear to be having its intended impact, slowly bringing along jurisdictions that otherwise would be lagging when it comes to legalizing housing, one by one.

articles.title: The Stranger’s Noise Complaint: XOË
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Welcome to Noise Complaint, The Stranger ‘s new audio and video music podcast featuring live performances right here at The Stranger HQ. Streamed live and released every other Friday, we invite a great band, musician, or wonderfully weird act to perform. Tune in, discover something new, and support art in your city.

The output of XOË—Zoë Duarte (vocals), Max Irvine (keyboards, guitar), Saba Samakar (drums), Adrian Michael (bass, guitar, drums)—is small so far, but it instantly ensnares you in its charms. Capturing a big chunk of your attention is the slyly seductive grain of Duarte’s voice, which, incidentally, is summarized by the title of their fantastic song “Sweet Sensation.” XOË (pronounced “X-O-E”) really blossom on their most recent release, the stellar Blur of a Dream EP; the slow-motion whirlpool of “Feed Me” is as dankly alluring as early Tricky. The earlier track “Nighttime Blues” bears the erotic mesmerism as Scritti Politti’s “The ’Sweetest Girl.’” Boudoir-friendly R&B may be the band’s dominant mode, but Irvine’s capable of florid keyboard arabesques worthy of jazz legends George Duke and Chick Corea. XOË even have a savvy interpretation of Nick Drake’s dream-folk classic “Pink Moon” in their arsenal. It’s certain that they have even more wonderful surprises for us on the horizon. DAVE SEGAL

articles.title: SIFF Cinema Workers Union Say Management Has ‘Unilaterally Suspended’ Bargaining
articles.author: Chase Hutchinson
paras: It’s been a great year for independent movie theaters in Seattle. But not for the workers in the SIFF Cinema Workers Union (SCWU). For the majority of 2026, they’ve been operating without a contract and bargaining has been slow going. Now, they say it’s been brought to a standstill. On top of that, SCWU claims management has retaliated against a union member, a charge SIFF disputes.
SCWU has filed an unfair labor practice (ULP) with the National Labor Relations Board—their second this year—over these issues and say they are now “actively discussing next steps.”

In a statement, the union said SIFF “unilaterally suspended the bargaining process” and “no progress has been made since the summer.” Back then, members expressed cautious optimism that SIFF was bargaining fairly after union members walked out before sold-out 70mm screenings of The Odyssey at SIFF Cinema Downtown. After providing management with a proposal in late August on the remaining issues in their contract and giving SIFF “extra time” to return to the union with a counterproposal, SIFF hasn’t been forthcoming at the subsequent meetings. They now say that SIFF abruptly canceled a meeting scheduled earlier last month “hours before it was meant to start” and haven’t scheduled any additional bargaining meetings since.

In response to a request for a comment and questions about the current state of contract negotiations, a spokesperson for SIFF said “there are next steps in the process but that is a conversation between the SCWU and SIFF, so we have no further comment at this time.” Previously, the organization said that it was “committed to good faith bargaining,” pointing to the number of bargaining sessions they’d taken part in (21 as of August) over the past several months as a demonstration of this commitment.

In regards to the ULP, the spokesperson said “SIFF welcomes the NLRB review of the ULP complaint as we are confident that they will find it baseless.” Asked where this confidence comes from and if they were similarly confident about the first ULP, which the NLRB has yet to rule on, the spokesperson declined to comment.

The union alleges that, in addition to outstanding concerns around transparency and what they say is “SIFF’s outright refusal to respond to a request for information regarding budgetary data,” management has retaliated against a member of union leadership.

“They gave this individual a ‘final warning’ within one disciplinary meeting, which violates the disciplinary rules set up in the contract,” Nico Hall, a SCWU member and member of the bargaining team, says. “The contract requires SIFF to gradually move an employee up several stages of discipline. Instead, SIFF has skipped through this process and placed this employee’s livelihood at risk.”

In response to the specific allegation of retaliation, a spokesperson for SIFF said they don’t “comment on any personnel matters,” but said that the organization “follows all internal processes as delineated in our employee handbook as well as the processes laid out in the agreement with the Union” and that “SIFF has not taken retaliatory action against any employee.”

Previously, the union has stopped short of calling for a boycott of SIFF or any of their theaters, which include SIFF Cinema Downtown, the SIFF Cinema Uptown, and SIFF Film Center. So far, they still aren’t calling for a boycott, but they won’t stop anyone who feels like boycotting.

“If SIFF customers feel motivated to boycott SIFF in response to their egregious mishandling of the bargaining process, SCWU would appreciate that support, especially if said customers send a message to SIFF warning them that their actions are losing business for the organization,” SCWU said in a statement.
